analytic.title: A Technique to Analyze the Tolerance to Transient Overloads of a Fault-Tolerant Real-Time System

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Fault-tolerance and real-time computing have been traditionally considered as different domains. However; missing a deadline is a fault in a real-time system. In this paper a real-time fault-tolerant architecture based on a Redundancy executive (RX) is presented. The timing properties of such an executive are predictable. On this basis, a technique for predicting the temporal behaviour of a systern, based oil fixed priority scliedulability analysis, is provided. Moreover; this analysis can be applied to real-time systems that present bounded transient overloads. In these systems the number of missed deadlines over a given period of time is bounded. The architecture, together with a dual time-out scheme, masks both value errors and timing errors. Thus, providing a feasible mechanism for achieving fault-tolerance for both the functional aspects and the timing aspects. Its application leads to cost-effective systems because the resources do not have to be sized for the worst case and, moreover; the response times are sometimes better than in the non-fault-tolerant equivalent system.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Two ways of achieving fault-tolerance are spatial redundancy and temporal redundancy. In temporal redundancy, altemative versions of a piece of code are executed whenever a fault occurs. With spatial redundancy, hardware is replicated, the same code (or different versions) execute in parallel and these versions vote upon the results. With temporal redundancy, it is very easy to mask transient faults as it is unlikely that the same fault will occur when reexecuting the code. Moreover, this approach does not require the use of replicated hardware that makes the system more expensive. On the other hand, spatial redundancy provides tolerance to both transient and permanent faults. The Pri-0-8 186-797 1 -9/97 $10.00 G 1997 IEEE mary/Backup (PB) scheme is an example of the temporal redundancy. The triple modular redundancy (TMR) is an example of the spatial redundancy [ 101. The approaches for integration of fault-tolerance in realtime systems can also be classified in the same terms. The work from Ghosh, Melhem and Moss6 [4] and the work from Liestman and Campbell [6] are examples of the PB approach. In their work a fault-tolerant scheduling algorithm to handle transient faults is presented. The tasks are assumed to be periodic, and short backup copies of all the tasks are scheduled on a uniprocessor system to guarantee a minimum of performance. The work from Oh and Son [9], on the other hand, presents a multiprocessor fault-tolerant strategy for periodic tasks. The work of Bernat, Mir6-JuliB and Proenza [3] is another example, in this work, redundant task sets run on different processors and the voting protocol allows to guarantee upper bounds on the response time of the result from the voter, thus deadlines can be guaranteed off-line.

The approach we present here is based on spatial redundancy and our aim is to provide off-line upper bounds on the total response times of the tasks that includes the time for performing the computations, exchanging the results and voting on them. Moreover, in this paper we show how to analyze the temporal behaviour of fault-tolerant real-time systems that allow transient overloads. A system is said to allow bounded transient overloads if it is admissible for it to miss a bounded number of deadlines over a period of time and consequently for a bounded amount of time.

Real-time systems that do not tolerate transient overloads have to be sized so that all deadlines will be met, even in the worst case. If bounded transient overloads are allowed, it is not required to size the design for the worst case, and this permits the creation of simpler and more cost-effective systems that make better use of the available resources. The schedulability analysis of transient overloads in simplex (non-redundant) systems can be done by a method developed recently [2]. We have extended the analysis to the case in which we have AT versions of the real-time system running in parallel. This redundancy will permit errors produced by a minority of the systems to be masked out. The masking is done by a special subsystem called the Redundancy executive (RX). The basic operation of the redundant system is as follows: some (or all) of the tasks that compose the real-time system will communicate with the RX. The RX will receive the results from these tasks, mask out any errors that have occurred and return a consensus result back to the versions. Once the versions have received the consensus result they will resume their computation. This is similar to the N-Version Programming paradigm [I], although in our study the N versions might be replicas instead of independently produced programs. The use of replicas will permit the tolerance of hardware and some transient software faults.

The time used for communication between the real-time system and the RX and the voting time should be bounded. With these constraints, upper bounds on the worst case response times of the tasks can be found. Existing faulttolerant architectures designed so that they can run NVP software either meet, or can easily be made to meet the constraints. These include centralized RX's, in the style of [5],
or distributed ones in the style of [8].

div.head: Faul t-tolerant Architecture
div.p: The technique we present in this paper will be useful for analyzing the temporal behaviour of a class of fault-tolerant real-time systems. These systems are those supported by an architecture that consists of Ai real-time nodes connected to a hardware device called the Redzritduncy eXecurive(RX) through a dedicated communication link. Each node will perform the same computations as the other ones, although not necesarilly using identical routines or algorithms. Periodically, it will pass partial results (cc-vectors) to the RX for voting, the RX will produce a consensus vector that will be returned to the nodes, then the computation will be resumed. This is similar to the N-Version Programming paradigm [ 11, although we do not necessarily consider the software to be diverse. The structure of the resulting architecture can be found in Figure l . We assume that in each node there is a set of periodic tasks carrying the computation (see next section). The end of a task is the natural point in which to interchange information and check if any fault has occurred. This is not necessary at the end of every task. For instance, we could have some very short tasks that read input data and we might not want to vote over the inputs. So the voting will take place at the end of only some of the tasks. In particular the voting process will be the main target of the schedulability analysis. It has to be possible to compute an upper bound on the maximum voting time. For this, we propose to use a dedicated processor for the voting (either centralized or distributed) scheduled with a fixed priority scheduler. The communication link will take an important role in the voting process so it must also adhere to predictability requirements: there has to be an upper bound on message transmission times. If links with message automatic retry in case of fault are considered, the time spent in the message retry has also to be bounded. The link could be either a set of point to point lines or a bus, but it will be, in any case, a dedicated link: only messages related with the voting process will use it. The objective of these requirements is to be able to compute off-line worst case response times and therefore apriori guarantees of the tasks temporal behaviour.

div.p: Based on the worst case response times @ ( k ) and l ? i ( k ) , we can compute the A i j ( k ) and the brotherhood A f i ( k * ) . Note that b?, ( k ) is the logical AND of M / ( k ) for all k of the brotherhood (see figure 2 a). For this reason we will call it the AND p-pattern. A 0 in any of the brothers implies a 0 in the brotherhood. Note that, while on a non fault-tolerant system the p-pattern is a one dimensional array, in the fault-tolerant model we have a bi-dimensional p-pattern. We note that in high assurance systems, it is as important to produce the correct results as to produce them on time. We introduce a time-out, called the D-time-out, to start a first voting process if a majority of the versions has arrived before the deadline expires. More precisely, at a time that, if the voter has received the data for voting from a majority of the nodes, it will have enough time to vote and send back the results to the nodes (also including additional interferences). If a majority consensus is reached, the correct result is produced on time. With D-timeouts the late versions are discarded for voting and they use the voting result of the other versions provided by the voter. If not enough versions are present at the D-timeout or the majority is not reached, then the versions wait until all versions finish or until the F-time-out, and then the voting is repeated.

For this mechanism to work propperly, it is essential to have different response times of the brothers at each invo- In this basic model, the analysis is very pessimistic due to the fact that the temporal behaviour of the brotherhood is of the slowest brother. In a non real-time context this can be an acceptable behaviour but in real-time systems, where guaranteeing deadlines is as important as providing correct results, this scheme is not adequate. Next section presents a dual time-out scheme that overcomes this problem.

div.head: Timeouts
div.p: Generally, fault-tolerant systems provide the mechanisms to define time-outs to avoid indefinite waiting for a task that has not finished. We propose the use of a dual time-out to avoid the indefinite waiting and to improve the number of deadlines met. We call them the F-time-out and the D-time-out.

The F-time-out is used to prevent tasks from waiting for other tasks that may have violated their worst case computation time. This time-out should be set at the latest time any version, under normal operation, would have finished, but not after next invocation time, to prevent voting tasks from interfering in an unbounded way with next task invocations. Using an F-time-out, we guarantee at run-time that at the end of each voting brotherhood invocation, either a consensus has been reached for all the tasks or no majority is reached. In this last case a safe shut-down is performed.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper we have addressed the problem of scheduling in real-time fault-tolerant systems. We have presented an architecture based on spatial redundancy to be used in real-time systems. The idea is to add a Redundancy eXecutive (RX) to current real-time nodes to achieve faulttolerance. The RX should include a voter (either centralized or distributed) and a dedicated communication link to communicate the nodes. Each of the components has to be predictable in order to be able to obtain off-line guarantees of the operation of the system.

We use an integrated scheduling approach based on fixed priority scheduling to analyze the worst case response time of the tasks in the system. We also assume that transient overloads are permitted and defined in terms of the n in 771 temporal constraint. This allows to have more cost-effective systems that make better use of available resources.

The worst case response time formulation developed shows that upper bounds of the tasks response times can be obtained, and off-line behaviour of the tasks predicted. Moreover, by using a dual time-out scheme not only data fault-tolerance is achieved but also tasks that miss the deadlines can be masked by faster ones. The protocol also ensures that either a consensus of all the versions is reached or a safe shut-down is performed.

The authors are currently working on the design and implementation of a RX. The communication link is a CAN based network and the implementation of the voter is based on the 805 I family of processors.
